title: How to...get attention : the doorway to learning
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton begins with the idea that attention, or noticing with interest, is what switches on the brain's learning chain, and applies it to newly appointed heads and teachers who must decide what colleagues will notice about them. He offers seven pointers illustrated with stories from his own headships: attention can be given to bad things too, choose deliberately what you want noticed, tie it to others' interests, learn about people first, stand out from the noise, show the benefit of paying attention, and have a secure evidence base. His examples include a failed attempt to showcase a star teacher, years in which his curriculum-writing drive misdirected attention away from learning, buying every teacher's requested equipment, and a course that sent heads to a nature reserve. The summary is that leaders should be clear what they want attention on, and earn it by relevance, novelty and credibility.
points: Attention is not always good, because the brain learns whatever it notices, including demoralising or unhelpful things.
Leaders should decide in advance what they want colleagues to notice, since everything a new head does is noticed and starts shaping others' impressions.
Gaining attention requires understanding people's interests first, and Skelton's early moves as head were buying requested resources and asking daily how the learning went.
Breaking expectations, as with a lavish prize or a walk in a nature reserve, can make a message stand out from the noise.
People attend to threats and to benefits, so leaders must show benefits and have a secure evidence base before asking for attention.
quotes: It is attention - noticing with interest - that turns on the cell body that causes everything else, - the neurons, the axon and the dendrites in our brain - to do their hard-wired things and, after repeated experiences, to make that new stuff sticky.
Their brains, remember, are always on. When someone new comes into a school, colleagues, students and others are not just experiencing; they are also paying attention.
What we mistakenly drew their attention to was a standard of teaching that simply demoralised them.

I enabled my colleagues to notice, week after week, that I was the curriculum guy. By the time the learning penny finally dropped for me I had very successfully misdirected everyone’s attention to curriculum rather than learning.
It didn’t matter that great conversations about learning didn’t happen straight away. It mattered that all my colleagues knew what question mattered to me.
We pay attention to potential threats and we pay attention to potential benefits. Both cause us to pay attention.
More people will pay attention to us if we know our stuff, if we have an evidence base for what we say and if the evidence base is secure.
